title: Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages

concept.text: The innovation would be a complete optical communication link that moves information across a large chip or between chips within a computing package using only a few tens of femtojoules per delivered information bit. Electronic data would drive an optical modulator, travel through an integrated optical path, and return to electronic form at a receiver. The defining energy budget includes generating the light and operating the necessary electronics, rather than counting only the optical device.

The system boundary is essential. A low-energy modulator still needs a driver, a light source, an optical path with manageable losses, a detector and receiver electronics. The supplied review of Kawahara and colleagues’ 2025 transmitter paper illustrates the difference: its reported driver-and-modulator energy is 0.78 pJ/bit, while an estimate adding laser wall-plug power and modulator bias control reaches 2.1 pJ/bit on the transmitter side alone. Neither figure represents a complete electrical-input-to-electrical-output link.

The proposed advance combines low total energy, high throughput and dense integration. It does not require an optical transistor or an optical computer: electronic processors could continue computing while optical links carry their data. The retained title names the ambition; the concrete demonstration proposed below uses a whole-link ceiling of 50 fJ per delivered information bit, not a claim that such performance has already been achieved.

significance.text: If complete optical links reached this energy range at useful package distances, they could substantially reduce the energy spent moving information between computing and memory components. The supplied transmitter paper motivates optical interconnects through electrical-wiring power and connects small device footprints with parallel channel integration. Its experiment supports that motivation, but does not demonstrate the proposed whole-link energy or a package-wide density advantage.

Conditional architectural synthesis: lower communication energy and demonstrably higher interconnect density could give designers more freedom to distribute computation and memory across a package. More communication could fit within a given power and area budget, potentially making some distributed architectures practical that would otherwise spend too much energy moving their data. The analogy to replacing a scarce material with an abundant one describes this relaxation of an architectural constraint; it is a judgment about the opportunity, not a measured consequence.

The opportunity has important limits. Low energy does not remove propagation latency, contention, routing constraints or packaging limits, so distance would not automatically become a weak overall architectural cost. A density advantage must also be demonstrated against a specified electrical alternative. An optical transistor would neither be necessary for this communication breakthrough nor, by itself, establish that the complete interconnect budget had been solved.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is simultaneous achievement of very low electrical-to-electrical energy, high per-channel throughput and dense multi-channel integration in a working package. The reviewed transmitter result shows why improving a single device is insufficient: adding estimated laser and bias-control power substantially increases its energy, before receiver processing is included. The supplied evidence does not establish a complete link meeting the proposed target.

Engineering synthesis: the optical path must deliver enough light to the detector while spending very little electrical power generating it. Coupling loss, propagation loss and modulator loss increase the light that must be launched, while laser wall-plug efficiency determines the electrical cost of that light. Efficient modulation must therefore be paired with efficient light generation and low-loss integration. A small device-energy figure cannot compensate automatically for losses elsewhere in the path.

Engineering synthesis: drivers and receivers must operate at the target rate within the same tight budget. Detector capacitance, electrical parasitics, receiver sensitivity and noise affect the energy needed to recover data reliably. Equalization, clocking, bias or thermal control, and error correction can consume energy and reduce useful throughput. Packaging must preserve alignment, optical performance and channel density across operating conditions and manufactured devices; these are system constraints, not merely modulator design goals.

The research attributes to Miller’s 2009 analysis an optical output-device target near 10 fJ/bit, detector capacitances of a few femtofarads and a need for dense waveguides. No retained document was supplied for that DOI, so the review could not verify the numerical targets, their exact scope or their attribution. These remain qualified historical reference points, distinct from the proposed whole-link target of 50 fJ per delivered information bit.

current_state.text: In a preprint submitted on June 5, 2025, Kawahara, Tsuchizawa, Yamamoto, Maegami, Yamada, Hara and Baba reported a co-packaged silicon slow-light modulator and current-mode driver operating at 64 Gbaud, with 0.78 pJ/bit for the driver and modulator and an active footprint of 0.66 mm². The reviewed text identifies NRZ operation at 64 Gb/s. The footprint is an active transmitter footprint, not a complete-link package area. The energy is 780 fJ/bit, or 78 times a 10 fJ/bit reference; that arithmetic does not verify the historical attribution of the reference.

The lowest-energy operating result required receiver equalization. Its bit-error rate was statistically estimated from fitted eye histograms and judged compatible with a forward-error-correction threshold; it was not a demonstration of a complete link running the required error correction with a measured residual error rate. The 0.78 pJ/bit figure excludes laser power and receiver processing, so it cannot be compared directly with a whole-link, delivered-information-bit target without accounting for those additions and any coding overhead.

The paper separately estimates 80 mW of laser electrical power using an assumed 20% wall-plug efficiency. Adding laser power and modulator bias control produces its estimated transmitter-side total of 2.1 pJ/bit. This is an estimate with stated assumptions, not a measured complete-link energy. It is nevertheless useful evidence that the light source and control circuits materially change the budget.

The supplied review had an untruncated ten-page text extraction of the preprint, including methods, results, appendices and references, as well as its abstract landing page. The landing page alone provides only partial access to the paper’s content. Figures were not visually inspected in the review; the findings retained here rely on statements in the extracted prose. The research also records a journal version associated with IEEE document 11278607 and a December 5, 2025 publication date, but no text from that document was retained, leaving the journal-version details unverified in this record.

The research separately reports a monolithic electronic–photonic transceiver at 128 Gb/s and 3.07 pJ/bit, excluding the laser, attributed to Optics Express 33, pages 46726–46738, dated October 27, 2025. No retained text for the cited DOI was supplied, so the review could not verify the result, publication details or energy boundary. This remains a reported result awaiting source verification; missing source text is not evidence that it is false.

As of the record’s November 1, 2026 reference date, the supplied material does not establish whether complete package links operating at a few tens of femtojoules per bit had been demonstrated. There is no retained bounded search record supporting the earlier statement that such links were not found. The reviewed June 2025 transmitter result remains valid within its stated scope, but neither that result nor the incomplete source collection establishes the latest field-wide performance.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a packaged multi-channel link between chips, or across a large die, at at least 100 Gb/s per channel and no more than 50 fJ per delivered information bit measured from electrical input to electrical output. Define whether the rate is net information throughput or gross signaling rate and report both. These thresholds are proposed criteria for this innovation, not an established standard or a demonstrated level of feasibility.
completion_criteria.label: Packaged channels achieve ≥100 Gb/s and ≤50 fJ/delivered-bit electrical-to-electrical

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting and reliability protocol: count laser wall-plug power, modulator drivers, detectors and receivers, required control circuits, equalization, clocking and forward-error correction. State how shared laser or control power is allocated across channels and how coding overhead changes the number of delivered information bits. Specify the correction scheme, measure pre- and post-correction error performance, and report residual errors over a stated traffic volume and duration. An inferred pre-correction BER below a coding threshold would be supporting evidence, rather than completion of this protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Full link energy accounting and measured residual post-correction errors

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical and reproducibility checks: report channel count, reach, optical losses, package area, simultaneous channel operation, traffic pattern, temperature range and tuning requirements. Repeat the result across multiple devices and packages, and provide enough design and measurement detail for independent reproduction. If higher density is part of the claimed breakthrough, compare aggregate useful bandwidth per stated area or package boundary with a specified electrical link under comparable reach, power and reliability conditions. The demonstrated operating range should define the practical claim; finite tests establish breadth within those conditions, not universal performance.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-device and multi-package reproducibility with reported practical operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPT-01, “Cascadable few-photon optical transistor,” concerns optical switching or gain that can drive subsequent optical stages. OPT-09 concerns transporting data efficiently between electronic endpoints and does not require such a transistor. Both involve optical signal control, but transistor operation would not establish a complete interconnect’s energy, reliability or density.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-03, “Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow,” has the most direct component overlap. A suitable integrated laser could contribute to the light source and packaging solution for OPT-09. CMOS-compatible laser fabrication alone would not demonstrate the laser efficiency, optical losses or complete-link energy required here.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-02, “Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold,” and OPT-10, “Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras,” overlap through photon generation, loss management and detection. Their objectives concern deterministic sources and photon-counting imaging, respectively. OPT-09 instead requires reliable data delivery at low total electrical energy; it does not inherently require deterministic single-photon emission or a photon-counting camera.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-07, “Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture,” shares broad concerns about controlling light and scaling many optical elements, but targets a programmable visible aperture rather than package data transport. OPT-05, “Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue,” and OPT-06, “Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic,” concern imaging performance. Their light-handling challenges do not make their completion criteria interchangeable with an interconnect’s energy, throughput and error requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-04, “Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source,” and OPT-08, “The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium,” share the broad field of optical engineering and physics but address different sources, interactions and experimental goals. Neither is an implied prerequisite for OPT-09. These relationships are inferred from the supplied roster titles; no supporting research for those entries was provided here.

change_log.change: Made the complete electrical-input-to-electrical-output link the defining concept and distinguished the retained title from the proposed 50 fJ demonstration ceiling.
change_log.reason: The innovation depends on the energy of all necessary components, and the title must not imply achievement.

change_log.change: Integrated the paper’s estimated 80 mW laser contribution, assumed 20% wall-plug efficiency and 2.1 pJ/bit transmitter-side estimate.
change_log.reason: The supplied full-text review adds material system-budget detail absent from the headline transmitter figure.

change_log.change: Qualified the Miller attribution while preserving the approximately 10 fJ/bit reference, few-femtofarad detectors and dense-waveguide requirements.
change_log.reason: No retained source text verifies those historical assertions; their uncertainty does not invalidate the whole-link concept.

change_log.change: Clarified the June 2025 result’s 64-Gbaud NRZ operation, 64-Gb/s rate, active footprint, equalization requirement and statistically estimated BER.
change_log.reason: These boundaries distinguish a transmitter experiment from a complete, error-corrected communication link.

change_log.change: Retained the journal-version and 128-Gb/s transceiver reports with explicit source-access limitations.
change_log.reason: Neither cited publication has retained text, so the reports cannot be verified or dismissed from this evidence.

change_log.change: Replaced the claimed absence of qualifying links with an unresolved assessment of field-wide performance as of November 1, 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied review contains no bounded freshness-search record supporting a negative literature conclusion.

change_log.change: Preserved the architectural opportunity and resource-abundance analogy while limiting claims about distance and density.
change_log.reason: Low energy does not eliminate latency or other communication constraints, and density requires a separate comparison.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to cover delivered-bit accounting, error correction, reproducibility, operating conditions and an electrical density benchmark.
change_log.reason: Energy and rate thresholds alone do not establish practical reliability, repeatability or the claimed density advantage.

change_log.change: Added distinctions for every other supplied roster entry without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: Related components and optical capabilities have different objectives and do not substitute for completion of OPT-09.

unresolved_issues: Miller’s exact 2009 numerical targets, terminology and intended device or system boundaries remain unverified.
The contents, publication date and relationship of IEEE document 11278607 to the reviewed preprint remain unverified.
The reported Optics Express transceiver’s 3.07 pJ/bit result, 128-Gb/s rate, laser exclusion and publication details require retained source text for verification.
The latest complete-link performance as of November 1, 2026 is unresolved because no bounded freshness-search evidence was supplied.
The feasibility of simultaneously meeting the proposed whole-link energy, rate and density goals is not established.
A test protocol still needs concrete channel count, reach, net-throughput definition, residual-error target, operating range, shared-power allocation and electrical comparison.
